titolo: Jensen Huang Is Back at Nvidia. Now Congress Wants Answers
angolo: The morning after: Huang's all-hands apology and therapy, the board under scrutiny, and the 12-day countdown to three Capitol Hill appearances.
descrizione: Jensen Huang Is Back at Nvidia. Now Congress Wants Answers. One day after the board reinstated him, Huang told employees he made 'terrible mistakes' and is in daily therapy, according to the New York Times and Bloomberg. House Democrats wrote to President Trump demanding to know what he knew and when. Huang faces closed House interviews on December 1 and a public Senate hearing on December 3. Here is what is confirmed, and what is only reported.

scene.testo: Monday, Nvidia's stock jumped more than thirty percent.
Its best day since May 2003.
Then, the next morning, Huang addressed his staff and apologized, according to Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the meeting.
Jensen Huang is back as CEO. But how did he sound on day one?

grafica.sotto: The questions Congress still wants answered

scene.testo: In a moment, the words he used with employees.
And a countdown with three dates on Capitol Hill.
First, what the board actually announced.
On November 23, Nvidia said Huang was reinstated as president and CEO.
Effective immediately, and as a member of the board.
The vote was unanimous, the company said.
The board said it received input from senior levels of the US government.
Based on that input, it is confident his return poses no national security risk.
That is the board's judgment, based on input it says it received from the government. It is not a finding by a court or agency.
Board chair Harvey Jones said the board believes Huang is the right person to lead Nvidia.
Interim CEO Colette Kress returns to her previous responsibilities as chief financial officer, Axios reports.
Remember the timing. Six days earlier, the chair said the opposite.
Even a company meeting days earlier went ahead without him, Bloomberg reports.
Huang co-founded Nvidia, which Bloomberg says he did about three decades ago.
Bloomberg calls Nvidia the world's largest chipmaker.
One analyst said he built a flat structure, making him hard to replace.
Then, on November 12, that world cracked.
Huang resigned on November 12 amid reports of affairs, according to the Washington Post and other outlets.
One reportedly involved a woman US officials suspect of being a Chinese spy.
But here's a detail that matters. Suspected is not proven.
CNN's sources said intelligence so far doesn't prove she spied for Beijing.
Attorney General Todd Blanche did not say whether federal investigators interviewed Huang or examined his relationship with the woman, and said officials must rely on actual intelligence assessments.
ABC, citing sources, reported contact with China's Ministry of State Security.
The FBI had been investigating the affair for at least a year, CNN reported.
Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe secrets were compromised.
Then came the market sell-off, and then a campaign to bring him back.
Axios reports a campaign backed by Trump, Elon Musk and other tech leaders pushed for his return.
President Trump repeatedly urged the board to bring Huang back, Axios reports.
On Sunday, Huang and the board held a second meeting, CNBC reports.
The Wall Street Journal reports Huang admitted to more affairs than previously reported in a meeting with the board before his reinstatement.
Monday, Trump spoke to CNBC and described his role.
Here is what he said.

citazione.testo: I spoke to them, let me put it that way. And I convinced them.

scene.testo: The Wall Street Journal reports he said he had communicated with the board directly and indirectly.
Huang later told staff he was not reinstated because he is a 'tech bro' above the law, according to Bloomberg's sources.
Now, the all-hands meeting.
It was Tuesday, and it lasted about an hour, according to reports.
Bloomberg reports he struck a somber tone.
According to reports, he apologized for violating Nvidia's code of conduct.
In the New York Times' account, as reported by The Hill, his words were direct.
The Times reported he said he was unfaithful to his wife, hurt his kids and hurt his colleagues.
He also told staff he is in therapy every day.
According to Bloomberg's sources, he insisted he wasn't reinstated because he's a 'tech bro' above the law.
According to Bloomberg's sources, he said the board would hold him to account going forward.
These accounts come from people familiar with the meeting, not a public recording.
According to The Hill's report, he said the board evaluated the entire situation and gathered facts after also receiving assurances from the Trump administration.
But the apology didn't settle Washington. It started a new fight.
Lawmakers from both parties criticized the reinstatement, NBC News and others report.
Trump told CNBC the board asked for assurance on the national security threat, and that his administration gave assurances 'with everything we know'.
He said, 'we believe he's fine.'
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer vowed Democrats 'will wield their full power to investigate' any wrongdoing, CBS News reports.
Some Democrats, such as Sen. Ruben Gallego, alleged a link to a donation to the president's ballroom, The Hill reports.
Those are Democrats' allegations. Nothing in these sources proves wrongdoing.
It isn't only Democrats. Republicans pushed back too.
Senator John Cornyn publicly questioned the claim of no national security risk.
Senator Kevin Cramer said on CNBC, 'We might even have to put a babysitter on Jensen Huang.'
Axios reports investors are concerned about how much time Huang will have to spend in front of Congress.
Now, the question about security clearance.
CBS News reported Huang still holds a security clearance, citing multiple sources.
Attorney General Todd Blanche did not say whether investigators interviewed him, CBS reports.
Trump says his administration gave the board assurances. That is not a formal finding.

visivo.testo: Trump says his administration gave the board assurances. That is not a formal finding.

scene.testo: And the board's own investigation is still open.
Nvidia says an independent committee will proceed to conclusion.
It also formed a National Security and Export Control Committee.
And it's searching for a new chief compliance officer.
Nvidia says it will keep cooperating with government investigations.
Reports say a network of firms moved advanced chips toward China.
Those are allegations from outlets and lawmakers. They are not court findings.
Now the countdown. Three dates, all within three days.
December 1: a closed-door, transcribed interview with three House committees.
Foreign Affairs, the Select Committee on the CCP, and Intelligence.
December 2: Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, follows.
December 3: a public Senate Banking Committee hearing.
The House chairs said they need answers on Nvidia's role.
Huang and Teter agreed to appear voluntarily, after the committees warned a subpoena could follow.
Senator Elizabeth Warren said Huang, executives and the board still owe Congress answers about export controls compliance.
So what does the stock jump tell us about this story?
CNN reports it was Nvidia's best day since 2003.
Nearly one trillion dollars in market value was added in one day, according to Yahoo Finance.
Critics say markets cheered, but national security questions remain open, NBC reports.
Here is what is confirmed. The board reinstated him, unanimously, by its own statement.
Confirmed: three appearances are scheduled on Capitol Hill, December first through third.
Reported, not confirmed by Nvidia: the apology and therapy, according to people at the meeting.
Still unknown: what Congress will learn, and what the board's probe finds.
Huang is back at the top, but the questions have just begun.
This story is still moving. Subscribe, and follow the countdown to December third.
